Charitable-donation statistics: a claimant count, a median and a total tell different stories

Explore official 2022 and 2023 donation-claim data, separate claimant counts from participation rates, and compare reported medians with approximate means derived from published totals.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Choose a source year. Compare the measures.

Fixed official 2022/2023 extract from Statistics Canada’s release of 1 April 2025, reviewed 25 October 2026. The control selects a reported tax year; it does not change an assumption or generate a forecast. The population is tax filers reporting claimed charitable donations in the preliminary T1 Family File, not all residents or everyone who gave. Published total amounts are in thousands of nominal CAD and are multiplied by 1000 for dollar charts. Medians condition on claiming tax filers. The age chart uses only the source’s Both sexes section. Means are derived from rounded official totals divided by reported claimants, then rounded to the nearest dollar; they are approximate calculations, not separately reported official means. Canada appears in headline metrics, while jurisdiction charts contain only provinces and territories. Claimed donations may relate to earlier gifts and spousal pooling. Unreceipted and other unclaimed giving is outside this release. No confidence bounds, personal giving target, tax credit or 2024 observation is invented.

The central idea

Check who is counted and what the denominator means. A tax-return claim is not a complete record of giving, and a national average is not a personal donation target.

01

Identify the people and the event being measured

Statistics Canada’s Charitable donors, 2023 release uses the preliminary T1 Family File. It describes charitable donations reported on tax returns, rather than every act of giving. This article retains its published 2022 and 2023 observations and was reviewed on 25 October 2026.

The source covers claims supported by official receipts for charities and approved organizations. It does not capture every small gift, unclaimed receipt or donation to an individual through crowdfunding. Nor does it count volunteering as a dollar donation.

The year control selects a tax year in this dated extract. It does not forecast giving or estimate a family’s tax credit. Keep the source population visible before comparing a chart with a household’s records: claiming tax filers, residents and people who actually gave are different groups.

02

A large claimant count does not establish a high participation rate

The first chart shows counts for the provinces and territories. Larger jurisdictions can have more claimants simply because they contain more people. A count alone does not tell us the share of that jurisdiction’s tax filers who reported a donation.

That share would require a matching denominator: all relevant tax filers in the same place and year. Dividing by a household count, a population estimate from another year or the Canada claimant total would answer a different question. This chart does not manufacture a denominator from unrelated data.

The national total is displayed separately from the jurisdiction bars. Canada is not another region to add to its constituent parts. Published counts and amounts are rounded, so small differences between an aggregate and a sum of displayed components should not be interpreted as missing individual records.

03

Keep units and claim timing beside the amount

The source table reports total donations in thousands of dollars. The dollar charts multiply those entries by 1,000. This unit conversion is essential: a table entry of 2,172,850 represents CAD 2,172,850,000, rather than CAD 2,172,850.

These are nominal amounts. The charts make no inflation adjustment and do not report a percentage of household income. A change in aggregate claims can reflect a change in claimant numbers, claimed amounts or their composition; the total alone cannot identify every driver.

The date a donation is claimed can also differ from the date cash left a bank account. The release explains that claims can include earlier gifts carried forward and donations pooled between spouses. The extract therefore should not be read as a complete calendar of cash paid to charities during the selected year.

04

Read a reported median separately from a derived mean

The reported median is the middle amount among the claiming tax filers in the group. It is not a donation made by the average resident. A higher regional median does not, by itself, establish a higher participation rate, a larger total or greater generosity.

A mean answers another question: total claimed dollars divided by claimant count. Using the published Canada totals gives an approximate mean of CAD 2,532 for 2023, compared with the reported median of CAD 390. The derived mean is rounded to the nearest dollar because the published inputs are themselves rounded.

The age chart repeats that calculation within each reported age group and uses the source’s Both sexes section. A large mean–median difference does not reveal every individual amount or the exact shape of the distribution. Neither statistic is a suggested gift, and neither determines what a household can afford.

05

Compare like groups without turning descriptions into causes

The age groups remain in their published order. Each median and derived mean conditions on claiming tax filers in that age band. Comparing those values does not show what would happen to the same person’s donations as they became older.

Income, wealth, family circumstances, tax-claim choices and other group differences can matter. The chart does not isolate those factors or estimate a causal age effect. It also supplies no confidence band or individual prediction.

Do not average the group medians to recreate a national median. Likewise, an unweighted average of group means would give a small claimant group the same influence as a large one. A national mean requires the national total divided by the national claimant count, or an appropriately weighted calculation using compatible group data.

06

Use the statistics as context for a separate giving plan

For a household plan, keep a record of gifts paid, receipts received and amounts claimed in each tax year. Those records answer different questions. A cash budget needs the dates money leaves; a tax claim needs the applicable receipt and reporting treatment.

The related giving-budget guide models personal payment timing separately. A published median cannot set an affordable commitment, and a tax-credit assumption does not supply cash before it is received. Begin with the household’s priorities and other obligations rather than treating a regional comparison as a target.

This extract is dated. The release states that a redesign delayed the 2024 reference-year release to winter 2026/2027. Recheck the official publication schedule before calling these figures the latest available. No missing year is invented or interpolated here, and two annual observations are not extended into a long-term forecast.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. All four charts use a fixed 2022/2023 official tax-data extract. The age-group means are explicitly derived approximations; the year control selects source observations rather than a hypothetical scenario. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
